sections.heading: Glossary term: Magnitude
sections.body: In astronomy, the magnitude is a measure of how bright  a celestial object is. The magnitude system used in astronomy originated in antiquity as a ranking of stars from the brightest to the least bright. That is why a smaller (or more negative) magnitude value means that the object is brighter, and a larger number means a fainter object. Hence a star with magnitude -1 is brighter than a star with magnitude 0 which in turn is brighter than a star of magnitude 1. Magnitude has a logarithmic scale, in which a magnitude difference of five corresponds to a factor of 100 difference in the amount of energy received: a star with magnitude 10  is a hundred times dimmer than a star with magnitude 5. There are different types of magnitude: apparent magnitude measures the apparent brightness of an object, which depends both on the object's luminosity – how much light the object emits – and on its distance from Earth. In contrast, the absolute magnitude is the value we would obtain if the object were at a standard distance of 10 parsecs (32.6 light years) from Earth. (For reflecting objects such as asteroids, there is a different definition.) In practice, magnitude is specified for observations through a specific filter, corresponding to an object's brightness in a given wavelength range of light. Numerous "photometric systems" for specifying filters, and corresponding magnitudes, exist.  In contrast, the bolometric magnitude is a direct measure of the luminosity of an object: the total electromagnetic energy emitted in unit time. Visual magnitudes correspond to the brightness as perceived by the human eye.

Glossary term: Magnitude

Description: In astronomy, the magnitude is a measure of how bright a celestial object is. The magnitude system used in astronomy originated in antiquity as a ranking of stars from the brightest to the least bright. That is why a smaller (or more negative) magnitude value means that the object is brighter, and a larger number means a fainter object. Hence a star with magnitude -1 is brighter than a star with magnitude 0 which in turn is brighter than a star of magnitude 1.

Magnitude has a logarithmic scale, in which a magnitude difference of five corresponds to a factor of 100 difference in the amount of energy received: a star with magnitude 10 is a hundred times dimmer than a star with magnitude 5.

There are different types of magnitude: apparent magnitude measures the apparent brightness of an object, which depends both on the object's luminosity – how much light the object emits – and on its distance from Earth.

In contrast, the absolute magnitude is the value we would obtain if the object were at a standard distance of 10 parsecs (32.6 light years) from Earth. (For reflecting objects such as asteroids, there is a different definition.)

In practice, magnitude is specified for observations through a specific filter, corresponding to an object's brightness in a given wavelength range of light. Numerous "photometric systems" for specifying filters, and corresponding magnitudes, exist. In contrast, the bolometric magnitude is a direct measure of the luminosity of an object: the total electromagnetic energy emitted in unit time. Visual magnitudes correspond to the brightness as perceived by the human eye.

Term and definition status: This term and its definition have been approved by a research astronomer and a teacher

The OAE Multilingual Glossary is a project of the IAU Office of Astronomy for Education (OAE) in collaboration with the IAU Office of Astronomy Outreach (OAO). The terms and definitions were chosen, written and reviewed by a collective effort from the OAE, the OAE Centers and Nodes, the OAE National Astronomy Education Coordinators (NAECs) and other volunteers. You can find a full list of credits here. All glossary terms and their definitions are released under a Creative Commons CC BY-4.0 license and should be credited to "IAU OAE".

sections.body_ru: В астрономии звёздная величина — это мера того, насколько ярким является небесный объект. Система звёздных величин, используемая в астрономии, возникла в древности как ранжирование звёзд от самых ярких к наименее ярким. Именно поэтому меньшее (или более отрицательное) значение звёздной величины означает, что объект ярче, а большее число означает более слабый объект. Следовательно, звезда с величиной -1 ярче звезды с величиной 0, которая, в свою очередь, ярче звезды с величиной 1. Звёздная величина имеет логарифмическую шкалу, в которой разница в пять величин соответствует различию в 100 раз в количестве получаемой энергии: звезда с величиной 10 в сто раз тусклее звезды с величиной 5. Существуют различные типы звёздных величин: видимая звёздная величина измеряет видимую яркость объекта, которая зависит как от светимости объекта — сколько света объект излучает — так и от его расстояния от Земли. Напротив, абсолютная звёздная величина — это значение, которое мы получили бы, если бы объект находился на стандартном расстоянии 10 парсек (32.6 световых лет) от Земли. (Для отражающих объектов, таких как астероиды, существует другое определение.) На практике звёздная величина указывается для наблюдений через определённый фильтр, соответствующий яркости объекта в заданном диапазоне длин волн света. Существует множество «фотометрических систем» для задания фильтров и соответствующих звёздных величин. Напротив, болометрическая звёздная величина — это прямая мера светимости объекта: полная электромагнитная энергия, излучаемая в единицу времени. Визуальные звёздные величины соответствуют яркости, воспринимаемой человеческим глазом.
